feedback.nudge: Sum down the columns of $G$ and set each to zero. Column $a$ has two non-zero entries and column $c$ has two; between them everything is in terms of $\pi_a$.

explanation:
## Solving $\pi G = 0$

Column by column:

$$\begin{aligned}
j = a:&\quad -2\pi_a + 1\cdot\pi_b + 0 = 0 &&\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_b = 2\pi_a\\
j = c:&\quad 0 + 2\pi_b - 3\pi_c = 0 &&\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_c = \tfrac23\pi_b = \tfrac43\pi_a
\end{aligned}$$

Column $b$ is then automatic: $2\pi_a - 3\pi_b + 3\pi_c = 2\pi_a - 6\pi_a + 4\pi_a = 0$. (It always is — the rows of $G$ sum to zero, so the columns of $\pi G$ sum to zero.)

Normalising, $\pi_a\bigl(1 + 2 + \tfrac43\bigr) = \tfrac{13}{3}\pi_a = 1$, so

$$\pi = \Bigl(\tfrac3{13},\ \tfrac6{13},\ \tfrac4{13}\Bigr), \qquad \pi_b = \frac{6}{13}.$$

## $\pi G = 0$, not $\pi P = \pi$

This is the one thing to get right about continuous time. In discrete time, stationarity is $\pi P = \pi$, equivalently $\pi(P - I) = 0$. The generator $G$ plays the part of $P - I$: it is the derivative of $P(t)$ at $t = 0$, and the stationarity condition is $\pi G = 0$.

Read as a balance equation, column $j$ says

$$\sum_{i \ne j} \pi_i g_{i,j} = \pi_j \sum_{k \ne j} g_{j,k},$$

that is, **the rate of probability flowing into $j$ equals the rate flowing out**. In continuous time these really are rates — probability per unit time — rather than per-step probabilities, which is why the diagonal is negative and the rows sum to zero rather than to one.

## What it does not say

$\pi$ is **not** the stationary distribution of the jump chain. The jump chain here has transition matrix

$$\tilde P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ \tfrac13 & 0 & \tfrac23\\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix},$$

whose stationary distribution is $\bigl(\tfrac16, \tfrac12, \tfrac13\bigr)$ — a different vector. The two differ because the continuous-time chain spends longer in states it leaves slowly: state $a$ has total rate 2 and so holds for $\tfrac12$ on average, while state $b$ has total rate 3 and holds for $\tfrac13$.

The relation between them is $\pi_i \propto \tilde\pi_i / g_i$, where $g_i$ is the total exit rate. Checking: $\tfrac16/2 : \tfrac12/3 : \tfrac13/3 = \tfrac1{12} : \tfrac16 : \tfrac19$, which scales to $3 : 6 : 4$. As it should.

## What the numbers are good for

By Theorem 5.19, $\P(X(t) = b) \to \tfrac6{13}$ from any start, and the long-run fraction of **time** spent at $b$ is $\tfrac6{13}$. The mean return time to $b$ is $m_b = 1/(\pi_b g_b) = 1/(\tfrac6{13}\cdot3) = \tfrac{13}{18}$ — note the extra factor of $g_b$, which is not there in discrete time and is the other place the holding rates show up.
